title: Vectors & Vector Spaces
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A vector is a quantity with magnitude and direction, represented as an ordered list of numbers (components). Vector operations: addition (component-wise), scalar multiplication (scaling). The dot product (a·b = Σaᵢbᵢ) measures alignment and gives length (‖v‖=√(v·v)) and the angle between vectors. Vectors live in vector spaces — sets closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Linear combinations build new vectors from others. This is the foundation: nearly all of data science, graphics, and ML represents data as vectors.

WORKED EXAMPLE: For vectors a=(1,2) and b=(3,4), the dot product = (1)(3)+(2)(4) = 3+8 = 11. If the dot product were 0, the vectors would be perpendicular (orthogonal). The dot product quantifies how much two vectors point the same way — the basis of similarity measures in search engines and recommendation systems.

PRACTICE: 1) Add (2,3) + (1,−1). 2) Compute the dot product of (1,0,2) and (3,1,1). 3) Find the length of the vector (3,4).

title: Matrices & Matrix Operations
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers — it encodes a linear transformation (a function that maps vectors to vectors, preserving lines and origin). Matrix addition (component-wise) and scalar multiplication. Matrix multiplication (row-by-column dot products) composes transformations — order matters (AB ≠ BA generally). The identity matrix I acts like 1. Matrix-vector multiplication transforms a vector. Dimensions must match for multiplication. Matrices are the fundamental computational object of the field — every neural network layer is a matrix multiplication.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Multiply [[1,2],[3,4]] by vector [5,6]: row 1 = (1)(5)+(2)(6)=17; row 2 = (3)(5)+(4)(6)=39. Result: [17,39]. The matrix transformed the input vector into a new one. Stacking such transformations (matrix products) is exactly how data flows through the layers of AI models — matrices in, matrices out, billions of times.

title: Systems of Linear Equations
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A system of linear equations can be written as Ax = b (matrix times unknown vector equals result). Gaussian elimination (row operations to reach row-echelon form) solves systems systematically. Solutions can be unique, none (inconsistent), or infinite (dependent). The augmented matrix combines A and b for elimination. Reduced row-echelon form (RREF) gives the solution directly. This connects to real problems: circuit analysis, economics, and fitting models to data all reduce to solving Ax = b.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Solve x + y = 5, x − y = 1. Add the equations: 2x = 6, so x = 3. Substitute: 3 + y = 5, so y = 2. As a matrix system, Gaussian elimination automates this for hundreds of variables. Every time you fit a line to data or balance a chemical equation, you're solving Ax = b — the workhorse of applied linear algebra.

PRACTICE: 1) Solve 2x + y = 7, x − y = 2. 2) Explain when a system has no solution. 3) Describe what row operations preserve.

title: Determinants & Inverses
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The determinant (det A) is a scalar that reveals key properties of a matrix: it measures how the transformation scales area/volume, and whether the matrix is invertible (det ≠ 0 means invertible). For 2×2 [[a,b],[c,d]], det = ad − bc. The inverse matrix A⁻¹ undoes A's transformation (AA⁻¹ = I); it solves Ax = b via x = A⁻¹b. A determinant of zero means the transformation collapses space (loses a dimension) and cannot be reversed — the matrix is 'singular.' Determinants also appear in cross products, eigenvalues, and change of variables.

WORKED EXAMPLE: For [[2,1],[3,4]], det = (2)(4)−(1)(3) = 8−3 = 5. Since det ≠ 0, the matrix is invertible. If det were 0, the transformation would squash 2D space onto a line, destroying information irreversibly. The determinant is a single number that tells you whether a transformation can be undone — profoundly useful in solving systems and analyzing stability.

PRACTICE: 1) Find the determinant of [[3,2],[1,4]]. 2) Explain what det=0 means geometrically. 3) State the condition for a matrix to be invertible.

title: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: An eigenvector of a matrix is a special vector whose direction is unchanged by the transformation — only its length scales, by a factor called the eigenvalue (Av = λv). Found by solving det(A − λI) = 0 (the characteristic equation). Eigenvalues reveal the 'natural axes' and scaling of a transformation. Diagonalization (A = PDP⁻¹) simplifies matrix powers and dynamics. Eigen-analysis is everywhere: Google's PageRank, principal component analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction, vibration modes, quantum mechanics, and the stability of dynamical systems.

WORKED EXAMPLE: For a matrix that stretches x-axis by 3 and y-axis by 2, the eigenvectors are the x and y axes themselves (their directions don't rotate), with eigenvalues 3 and 2. PCA uses this: it finds the eigenvectors of a data covariance matrix to discover the directions of greatest variance, compressing high-dimensional data while preserving structure — the mathematical heart of dimensionality reduction.

title: Orthogonality & Projections
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Orthogonal vectors are perpendicular (dot product = 0). Orthonormal sets (perpendicular and unit length) form ideal bases. Projection drops a vector onto a subspace — finding the closest point (the shadow). The Gram-Schmidt process builds orthonormal bases. Least squares uses projection to find the best-fit solution when Ax = b has no exact solution (overdetermined systems) — this is how linear regression works. Orthogonal matrices preserve lengths and angles (rotations/reflections). Orthogonality makes computation stable and decomposition clean.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Fitting a line to scattered data points: no line passes through all of them (the system Ax=b is inconsistent). Least squares projects b onto the column space of A, finding the line minimizing the total squared distance to the points. This projection — pure linear algebra — is exactly the linear regression underlying much of statistics and machine learning. Orthogonality gives the 'best possible' answer when perfect is impossible.

PRACTICE: 1) Determine if (1,2) and (2,−1) are orthogonal. 2) Explain what a projection finds. 3) Describe how least squares relates to fitting data.

title: Grandmaster — Decompositions & Applications
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Matrix decompositions factor a matrix into simpler pieces, revealing structure and enabling computation. LU decomposition (lower×upper) speeds solving systems. QR decomposition (orthogonal×upper-triangular) powers least squares and eigenvalue algorithms. The Singular Value Decomposition (SVD): A = UΣVᵀ works for ANY matrix, revealing the fundamental geometry of a transformation — it underlies image compression, recommendation systems (Netflix), latent semantic analysis, and pseudo-inverses. These decompositions are how linear algebra is actually computed at scale in scientific computing and machine learning.

WORKED EXAMPLE: SVD compresses an image by keeping only the largest singular values (the most 'important' components) and discarding small ones — reconstructing a near-identical image with a fraction of the data. The same math powers recommendation engines: decomposing a user-item matrix reveals latent factors (hidden preferences). SVD is arguably the most useful matrix decomposition in all of applied mathematics — one tool, countless applications.

title: King Level — Linear Algebra as the Language of Modern Computation
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At the highest level, linear algebra is revealed as the computational foundation of the modern world — the mathematics that makes machine learning, computer graphics, data science, quantum computing, and scientific simulation possible. Every neural network is layers of matrix multiplications and nonlinear functions; training is gradient-based optimization over these matrices. High-dimensional vector spaces represent words (embeddings), images (pixel matrices), and data (feature vectors). Abstract vector spaces generalize beyond arrows to functions, polynomials, and signals. The King-level truth: when computers 'understand' language or 'see' images, they are performing linear algebra — the deceptively simple operations of scaling, adding, and transforming vectors, executed at massive scale, are what create the appearance of intelligence. Mastering linear algebra is mastering the actual mechanism beneath the AI revolution.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A large language model represents each word as a vector in a high-dimensional space (an embedding). Words with similar meanings have vectors pointing in similar directions (measurable by dot product). The model's 'reasoning' is a sequence of matrix transformations of these vectors. When it seems to understand language, it is multiplying matrices and computing dot products — the exact operations in this course, scaled to billions of parameters. Linear algebra is not a prerequisite to AI; it IS AI's substrate.
